references.text: Isaiah's parable of the vineyard is the background for Jesus' parable about the vineyard. In Isaiah 5:1-7, the prophet describes Israel as the Lord's vineyard, and God threatens to destroy it because it produced bad fruit. Jesus builds upon this image.

In Matthew's parallel account, the listeners themselves answer the question of what the owner of the vineyard will do: 'He will bring those wretched men to a wretched end and lease out the vineyard to other tenants' (Matthew 21:41-43). Jesus adds that the kingdom of God will be taken from them and given to a people who produce its fruit.
The parallel passage in Mark 12:9 has the same content: The owner of the vineyard will come, destroy the tenants, and give the vineyard to others.

Paul and Barnabas tell the Jews in Antioch that God's word must first be spoken to them, but since they reject it, the apostles turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). This reflects the fulfillment of the vineyard being 'given to others'.
Paul explains in Romans 11:11-12 that Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles, which corresponds to the vineyard being given to other tenants.

The expression "Μὴ γένοιτο" (May it never be!) is used repeatedly by Paul, for example in Romans 9:14, as a strong rejection of an unwanted thought. In Luke 20:16, the listeners react with the same expression in horror at the idea that the vineyard will be taken from them.
In Deuteronomy 32:21, God says he will make Israel jealous by means of those who are not a people. This points to the theme that God's blessings are given to others when Israel is unfaithful.

Jesus' response to the listeners' 'May it never be!' follows immediately in Luke 20:17-18, where he quotes Psalm 118:22 about the stone the builders rejected and confirms the inevitability of judgment.
